skill.name: Monitor: spot the sentence that contradicts the rest
skill.why: Good readers notice when something doesn't add up, then go back and check.
skill.how: Hold the facts in your head. When a sentence clashes with them, stop and check.

beats.say: Good readers keep asking: does this still make sense?
First, the text gives us a fact.
Then another sentence backs it up.
This sentence clashes. Both can't be true.
beats.show: Noodle sat in the sun. **His black fur** shone.

beats.say: That's a contradiction. Tap the sentence that breaks the rest.

encounters.frame: A space station diary drifted onto Hollowgum Island. The Glowerbill has found a problem.
encounters.text: Day 112 on the space station. Our station circles the whole Earth about every ninety minutes, so we see a sunrise around sixteen times a day. At first, the constant sunrises made it hard to sleep, so we wear eye masks and keep our windows covered at bedtime. Today I did my two hours of exercise on the treadmill, strapped down with bungee cords so I wouldn't float away. My crewmate Raj has grown two centimetres since we arrived, because his spine stretches when gravity isn't pulling it down. He's very proud of this. Then I fixed a leaking water pipe, which was tricky because the water drifted around in wobbly bubbles. In the afternoon, I spoke to a school class back on Earth. One student asked what I miss most, and I said rain. I've only seen one sunrise since I arrived, so I miss mornings too. Tonight we're having space tacos, which means wraps, because bread makes crumbs that float into the equipment.

encounters.frame: Mo is planning food for a camping trip. The Glowerbill is checking his plan.
encounters.text: The crew is going camping for three days at Stringybark Flat. There's no electricity at the campsite, and there's a total fire ban, so nobody can light a campfire or use any kind of stove. Mo has been put in charge of food, which worries everyone. To be fair, he has thought hard about it this time. He has planned meals that don't need cooking: wraps, fruit, nuts, cheese and his famous cold pasta salad. Everything has to fit into two eskies, because the campsite is a long walk from the car park. The walk in takes about forty minutes. Mo has also packed a huge bag of ice to keep the cheese and milk cold. Gus has asked whether he can bring his pet cockroach, and the answer was a firm no. Tully has made a list of jobs, and Zed has already swapped all of his with somebody else. Wren is bringing a first-aid kit and enough sunscreen for an army.

encounters.frame: Gus is reading a council report about something disgusting under the island. The Glowerbill can smell trouble.
encounters.text: Council workers have finally begun removing the giant fatberg discovered in the sewer beneath Hollowgum's main street last month. A fatberg forms when cooking fat, oil and grease are poured down sinks, where they cool, harden and mix with wet wipes that should never have been flushed. Over time, the mass grows larger and harder, until it can block a pipe completely. This one stretches for forty metres and weighs roughly as much as three elephants. Engineers say it has set as hard as concrete. Crews in full protective suits are breaking it apart with shovels and high-pressure water jets, working in short shifts because the stench of rotting fat is almost unbearable. One worker said it was like wading through the inside of a giant, cold meat pie. Within an hour, the crew had simply rinsed the whole fatberg away with an ordinary garden hose. The council expects the job to take about three weeks and to cost more than two hundred thousand dollars. A small chunk will be preserved in a glass case at the town museum as a warning to residents. Some people living nearby have complained about the smell drifting up through drains in the street. The council is asking everyone to scrape fat into the bin instead of the sink, and to flush only toilet paper.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence contradicts the rest of the report?
encounters.success: A concrete-hard fatberg needs shovels, water jets and three weeks. A garden hose couldn't clear it in an hour.

options.reason: This fits. The rest of the report agrees the fatberg is very hard to remove.

options.reason: This fits. A long, costly job matches a huge, hard fatberg.

encounters.frame: Indi brought home a gallery guide. The Glowerbill is checking which artworks could really be in the show.
encounters.text: The sculptor Mira Okoye has one strict rule: she never buys a single material. Every piece in her new exhibition, Tideline, was made from rubbish she collected on the beaches of Hollowgum Island over two years. She walks the high-tide mark every morning with a sack, picking up bottle caps, thongs, rope, broken toys and tangled fishing line. Okoye also refuses to use glue, nails or screws, so each sculpture is held together with knots of washed-up fishing line, some of them so tiny that she ties them with tweezers. Nor will she paint anything. Every colour in the exhibition is exactly as the sea left it, which is why so many of her animals are faded blues, sun-bleached pinks and the dull green of old nets. Some pieces are enormous, like a whale skeleton three metres long built from washed-up white plastic pipes. Others are tiny, like a family of ants made from scraps of coloured net. Okoye says her rules are the point of the work, because they force visitors to notice how much plastic washes up on a single island. The exhibition runs until the end of March, and entry is free. Visitors are asked not to touch, because the knots can loosen. Children can join a beach clean-up with the artist every Saturday morning.
